81: **[SECTION 2 --- UCC ARTICLE 8 vs. ARTICLE 9 CONTROL LANGUAGE]{.underline}**
82: 
83: **[2.1 --- Pinnacle\'s Preferred Position (Green)]{.underline}**
84: 
85: Pinnacle\'s form ACA uses \"entitlement order\" language drawn from UCC Article 8 (specifically, UCC § 8-102(a)(8)) rather than the Article 9 \"instruction\" terminology found in UCC § 9-104(a)(2). This is a deliberate drafting choice that reflects Pinnacle\'s belt-and-suspenders approach to perfection of its security interest in controlled deposit accounts.
86: 
87: The rationale for using Article 8 language is as follows: if the deposit account can be characterized or re-characterized as a \"securities account\" within the meaning of UCC § 8-501 --- for example, because the account is a money market deposit account, a sweep account that invests in securities or money market instruments, or an account that holds financial assets credited to the depositor\'s account --- then control under Article 8 (via the securities intermediary\'s agreement to comply with \"entitlement orders\" as defined in UCC § 8-102(a)(8)) provides an additional layer of perfection beyond Article 9 control. Under UCC § 8-106(d), a purchaser (including a secured party) has \"control\" of a security entitlement if the securities intermediary has agreed to comply with entitlement orders originated by the purchaser without further consent of the entitlement holder. By incorporating this concept into the ACA, Pinnacle obtains dual-track perfection: control under Article 9 (as to the deposit account) and control under Article 8 (as to any security entitlement).
88: 
89: \"Entitlement order\" is defined under UCC § 8-102(a)(8) as a notification communicated to a securities intermediary directing transfer or redemption of a financial asset to which a specified person has acquired a security entitlement. Pinnacle\'s form ACA incorporates this term in Section 2(a) of the ACA, which provides that the bank agrees to comply with \"entitlement orders\" originated by the Secured Party with respect to the Accounts, thereby satisfying the control requirements of both UCC § 8-106 and UCC § 9-104. The operative provision of the form ACA reads, in relevant part:
90: 
91: > *\"The Bank agrees that it will comply with entitlement orders originated by the Secured Party with respect to the Accounts without further consent of the Depositor. For purposes of this Agreement, \'entitlement order\' has the meaning assigned to such term in Section 8-102(a)(8) of the UCC. The Bank further agrees that it will comply with instructions originated by the Secured Party directing disposition of the funds in the Accounts without further consent of the Depositor.\"*
92: 
93: This dual-track approach --- referencing both \"entitlement orders\" under Article 8 and \"instructions\" under Article 9 --- has been accepted by major depository banks in approximately 70% of Pinnacle\'s recent transactions without substantive objection. The remaining 30% of transactions have resulted in bank pushback, typically from bank counsel that maintains standardized ACA forms and resists deviations from their templates.
94: 
95: **[2.2 --- Common Bank Pushback]{.underline}**
96: 
97: The typical bank markup in this area involves the substitution of \"instruction\" (Article 9 terminology) for \"entitlement order\" (Article 8 terminology) in the operative control section of the ACA. The bank\'s position is generally that the controlled accounts are ordinary demand deposit accounts and not securities accounts, and that Article 8 terminology is therefore inapplicable and potentially misleading.
98: 
99: The bank\'s rationale is grounded in the following concerns: depository banks --- particularly those with standardized form ACAs reviewed by their own outside counsel --- resist Article 8 language because they do not wish to be treated as \"securities intermediaries\" within the meaning of UCC § 8-102(a)(14). Under Article 8, a securities intermediary is subject to a series of statutory duties, including the duty to comply with entitlement orders under UCC § 8-507, the duty to maintain a sufficient quantity of financial assets under UCC § 8-504, and the duty to exercise rights as directed by the entitlement holder under UCC § 8-506. Banks that are not in the business of maintaining securities accounts --- i.e., commercial banks as distinguished from broker-dealers and custodians --- are understandably reluctant to assume these additional obligations, which could alter the priority scheme applicable to the accounts and impose regulatory and operational burdens that the bank did not contemplate when establishing the deposit relationship.
100: 
101: Bank counsel (e.g., firms such as Blackmere Fox LLP, which has represented Ironbridge National Bank, N.A. in recent transactions) may cite OCC guidance or bank regulatory concerns as a basis for resisting securities-intermediary characterization. Some bank counsel have taken the position that characterizing an ordinary demand deposit account as a \"securities account\" could trigger regulatory reporting obligations or capital adequacy implications, although this argument is generally overstated and can be addressed by clarifying that the Article 8 language operates only as a conditional fall-back --- i.e., it applies only *if* the account is deemed to be a securities account, and does not independently re-characterize the account.
102: 
103: **[2.3 --- Acceptable Fallback Positions (Yellow)]{.underline}**
104: 
105: Two pre-authorized fallback positions are available for this issue category, presented in order of preference:
106: 
107: **Fallback A --- Dual-Track Compromise.** Accept the bank\'s substitution of \"instruction\" for \"entitlement order\" in the operative control section (Section 2(a) of the ACA), but add a standalone representation and covenant by the bank providing that if any Account is at any time deemed a \"securities account\" under UCC Article 8, the bank agrees to comply with entitlement orders originated by the Secured Party without further consent of the Depositor. This approach preserves the belt-and-suspenders protection while accommodating the bank\'s concern about day-one Article 8 characterization. The following sample language should be inserted as a new subsection:
108: 
109: > *\"Notwithstanding the foregoing, if any Account is at any time deemed to be a \'securities account\' (as defined in Section 8-501 of the UCC), the Bank agrees to treat the Secured Party as the \'entitlement holder\' (as defined in Section 8-102(a)(7) of the UCC) with respect to such Account and to comply with \'entitlement orders\' (as defined in Section 8-102(a)(8) of the UCC) originated by the Secured Party with respect to such Account without further consent of the Depositor.\"*
110: 
111: This language has been well received by bank counsel in prior transactions because it is explicitly conditional (\"if any Account is at any time deemed to be a \'securities account\'\") and does not, on its face, characterize the accounts as securities accounts or the bank as a securities intermediary. It addresses the bank\'s core concern while preserving Pinnacle\'s fallback Article 8 protection.
112: 
113: **Fallback B --- Article 9 Only with Protective Representation.** If the bank rejects Fallback A, accept Article 9-only \"instruction\" language throughout the operative control provisions, but require the bank to add a representation and covenant confirming that it has not entered into, and will not enter into, any agreement with any other party pursuant to which it agrees to comply with instructions or entitlement orders concerning any Account. This representation ensures that even without Article 8 belt-and-suspenders language, Pinnacle\'s Article 9 control is unimpaired by competing agreements that could affect priority under UCC § 9-327. The relevant sample language for this representation is set forth in Section 12 of this playbook (Representations and Warranties).
114: 
115: Fallback B is a meaningful concession and should be offered only if Fallback A has been expressly rejected by the bank. When offering Fallback B, the negotiator should present it as the final position on this issue and make clear that Pinnacle is not prepared to accept Article 9-only language without some form of protective representation regarding competing agreements.
116: 
117: **[2.4 --- Walk-Away / Escalation Triggers (Red)]{.underline}**
118: 
119: The following scenarios require escalation or represent hard-stop positions:
120: 
121: > • If the bank refuses both Fallback A and Fallback B and insists on \"instruction\"-only language without any protective representation regarding competing agreements, **escalate to Diana Whitford**. While Article 9-only language, standing alone, is sufficient for perfection, the absence of any representation regarding competing agreements creates a risk that the bank may have entered into (or may in the future enter into) a competing control agreement with another secured party, which could affect Pinnacle\'s priority under UCC § 9-327.
122: >
123: > • If the bank takes the position that the ACA does not confer \"control\" within the meaning of UCC § 9-104(a)(2) --- i.e., if the bank\'s markup conditions compliance with Pinnacle\'s instructions on depositor consent even after delivery of a NOEC --- this is a **hard stop**. Such language destroys perfection and cannot be accepted under any circumstances. The negotiator should escalate immediately to Thomas Orr and Diana Whitford and should consider engaging a replacement bank if the depository bank is unwilling to cure the deficiency.
124: 
125: **Guiding Principle:** Preserving valid \"control\" under UCC § 9-104 is non-negotiable. Any provision that makes the bank\'s compliance with Secured Party instructions contingent on Depositor approval post-NOEC delivery vitiates the control necessary for perfection and must be rejected outright, regardless of any other concessions the bank may offer on other issues.
126: 
127: **[SECTION 3 --- EXCLUSIVE vs. SPRINGING CONTROL MECHANICS]{.underline}**
128: 
129: **[3.1 --- Pinnacle\'s Preferred Position (Green)]{.underline}**
130: 
131: Pinnacle\'s form ACA uses a \"springing exclusive control\" model. Under this model, the control mechanic operates in two phases:
132: 
133: > **Phase 1 --- Pre-NOEC (Ordinary Course Operations).** Prior to the delivery of a NOEC by Pinnacle to the bank, the Depositor (e.g., Graycliff Industries, Inc.) is permitted to operate the controlled accounts in the ordinary course of business --- originating debits, credits, wire transfers, ACH transactions, and other transfers --- without Pinnacle\'s prior consent. During this phase, Pinnacle\'s control exists as a legal matter (because the bank has agreed to comply with Pinnacle\'s instructions without the Depositor\'s consent), but Pinnacle does not exercise that control on a day-to-day basis. The Depositor retains operational access to the accounts and uses them for working capital management, vendor payments, payroll, and other business purposes.
134: >
135: > **Phase 2 --- Post-NOEC (Exclusive Control).** Upon delivery of a NOEC by Pinnacle to the bank, exclusive control springs to Pinnacle, and the bank must cease complying with the Depositor\'s instructions and instead comply solely with Pinnacle\'s instructions regarding the disposition of funds in the controlled accounts. The Depositor\'s operational access is extinguished, and the bank must freeze the accounts (or redirect funds as directed by Pinnacle) until the ACA is terminated or the NOEC is rescinded.
136: 
137: The springing control model is preferred over day-one exclusive control for several reasons. First, it permits the borrower to operate its business without the operational burden of seeking Pinnacle\'s approval for each transaction in the controlled accounts, which would be commercially impracticable in a performing credit relationship. Second, it preserves Pinnacle\'s ability to lock down the accounts upon a triggering event --- typically the occurrence of an Event of Default under the Credit Agreement --- thereby protecting the collateral at the moment when protection is most needed. Third, the springing model is the market-standard approach in leveraged lending and middle-market credit transactions and is generally accepted by depository banks without fundamental objection.
138: 
139: The critical element of the springing control model --- and the element most frequently targeted by bank markups --- is the bank\'s unconditional agreement to comply with Pinnacle\'s instructions after NOEC delivery **without any requirement to obtain the Depositor\'s consent, verify the occurrence of an Event of Default, or otherwise qualify its compliance obligation.** The form ACA achieves this by providing:
140: 
141: > *\"Upon the Bank\'s receipt of a Notice of Exclusive Control delivered by the Secured Party in accordance with Section \[●\], the Bank shall comply exclusively with instructions of the Secured Party with respect to the Accounts and shall not comply with instructions of the Depositor with respect to the Accounts. The Bank shall not require the consent, approval, or authorization of the Depositor as a condition to its compliance with the Secured Party\'s instructions following receipt of a Notice of Exclusive Control.\"*
142: 
143: **[3.2 --- Common Bank Pushback]{.underline}**
144: 
145: Banks frequently push back on the springing control mechanic in two principal ways:
146: 
147: **Processing and Wind-Down Carve-Outs.** Banks commonly insert a carve-out allowing the Depositor to continue operating the accounts even after delivery of a NOEC unless and until the bank has had time to process and implement the NOEC through its internal systems. The bank\'s concern is operational: upon receipt of a NOEC, the bank must update its systems to redirect account access, disable the Depositor\'s online banking credentials, freeze automated payment templates, and coordinate across multiple internal departments (operations, compliance, legal, and relationship management). Some banks seek to retain the right to honor previously issued or pending Depositor instructions --- such as outstanding checks, ACH batches in process, wire transfers that have been initiated but not yet completed, and standing payment orders --- for a specified period after NOEC delivery.
148: 
149: **Certification of Default.** Some banks seek to add a requirement that the NOEC include a certification that an Event of Default has occurred under the Credit Agreement, or that the NOEC specify the nature of the triggering event. The bank\'s rationale is that it does not want to be placed in the position of freezing its customer\'s accounts based on an unsubstantiated instruction from the Secured Party, and that a certification provides the bank with a degree of assurance (and potential legal cover) that the NOEC has been properly issued.
150: 
151: Both of these pushback positions raise concerns, but they are not equally problematic. The processing carve-out is an operational issue that can be addressed through a limited wind-down period (see Fallback A below). The certification requirement, however, is a structural issue that must be firmly resisted, as discussed in Fallback B and the Red-tier triggers below.
152: 
153: **[3.3 --- Acceptable Fallback Positions (Yellow)]{.underline}**
154: 
155: **Fallback A --- Operational Wind-Down Period.** Accept a limited wind-down period --- not exceeding one (1) business day after the bank\'s receipt and confirmation of the NOEC --- during which the bank may honor Depositor instructions that were originated by and accepted by the bank prior to the bank\'s receipt of the NOEC. After the expiration of the wind-down period, the bank must comply exclusively with Pinnacle\'s instructions. This fallback acknowledges the operational reality that the bank cannot instantaneously freeze all account activity and allows a brief period for in-process transactions to settle. The following sample language may be offered:
156: 
157: > *\"The Bank shall comply with the Secured Party\'s instructions with respect to the Accounts commencing on the business day immediately following the Bank\'s receipt and confirmation of a Notice of Exclusive Control, provided that the Bank may honor instructions of the Depositor that were originated by and accepted by the Bank prior to the Bank\'s receipt of such Notice, but only to the extent such instructions have not been completed as of such time.\"*
158: 
159: Key drafting points for this fallback language: (i) the wind-down applies only to Depositor instructions that were *originated and accepted* before the NOEC was received --- the bank may not accept new Depositor instructions after NOEC receipt; (ii) the wind-down is limited to one business day; and (iii) after the wind-down, the bank\'s compliance with Pinnacle\'s instructions is exclusive and unconditional.
160: 
161: **Fallback B --- No Certification of Default.** The NOEC shall not be required to certify or specify the nature of the Event of Default or other triggering event; a statement by Pinnacle that it is exercising its rights under the ACA shall be sufficient. This position is non-negotiable even as a fallback --- it is a structural requirement, not a concession. The bank is not a party to the Credit Agreement and is not in a position to evaluate the occurrence or continuation of an Event of Default; imposing a certification requirement effectively delegates to the bank a contractual interpretation function that belongs exclusively to the Secured Party. Moreover, a certification requirement creates the risk that the bank will refuse to comply with a NOEC on the ground that the certification is incomplete or inaccurate, thereby undermining Pinnacle\'s ability to exercise control at the moment when it is most critical. The NOEC form attached to the ACA should contain a simple statement:
162: 
163: > *\"The Secured Party hereby notifies the Bank that the Secured Party is exercising its rights under Section \[●\] of the Account Control Agreement dated as of \[●\], and directs the Bank to comply exclusively with instructions of the Secured Party with respect to the Accounts.\"*
164: 
165: No additional certification, explanation, or supporting documentation should be required.
166: 
167: **[3.4 --- Walk-Away / Escalation Triggers (Red)]{.underline}**
168: 
169: The following positions represent escalation triggers or hard stops:
170: 
171: > • Any bank markup requiring the Depositor\'s consent to the NOEC, or requiring the bank to verify the occurrence of an Event of Default before complying with Pinnacle\'s post-NOEC instructions, is a **hard stop**. Such a provision is fundamentally inconsistent with UCC § 9-104(a)(2) control and vitiates perfection. Reject outright and escalate to Thomas Orr and Diana Whitford.
172: >
173: > • Any wind-down period exceeding two (2) business days --- **escalate to Diana Whitford**. While a one-business-day wind-down is the pre-authorized fallback, a two-business-day period may be acceptable in certain circumstances depending on the bank\'s operational constraints and the size of the controlled balances. Wind-down periods of three or more business days are presumptively unacceptable and require express deal-team approval.
174: >
175: > • Any carve-out permitting the bank to continue honoring *new* Depositor instructions (as opposed to previously originated instructions in process) after NOEC delivery --- **hard stop**. This is functionally equivalent to requiring the Depositor\'s consent and destroys the springing-control mechanic entirely.
176: 
177: **[SECTION 4 --- NOEC COMPLIANCE PERIOD]{.underline}**
178: 
179: **[4.1 --- Pinnacle\'s Preferred Position (Green)]{.underline}**
180: 
181: Pinnacle\'s form ACA requires the bank to begin complying with Pinnacle\'s exclusive instructions within two (2) business days of the bank\'s receipt of a NOEC. This two-business-day period represents the time allowed for the bank to process the NOEC through its internal systems --- including updating account access controls, freezing automated payment instructions, and coordinating across the bank\'s operations, compliance, and legal departments --- and to transition operational control of the accounts from the Depositor to the Secured Party.
182: 
183: The rationale for a two-business-day period is straightforward: speed of lock-down is essential in distressed situations. When Pinnacle delivers a NOEC, it is typically because the borrower has experienced an Event of Default --- which may include a payment default, a financial covenant breach, a material adverse change, or a triggering event under the Credit Agreement\'s acceleration provisions. In such circumstances, the borrower may be actively dissipating assets or diverting cash from the controlled accounts. Every additional business day between the NOEC and the bank\'s compliance with Pinnacle\'s exclusive instructions is a day during which the borrower can withdraw, transfer, or encumber the controlled deposit balances. A two-business-day compliance period balances the bank\'s legitimate operational needs against Pinnacle\'s need for prompt access to its collateral.
184: 
185: **[4.2 --- Common Bank Pushback]{.underline}**
186: 
187: Banks commonly request a longer compliance period, typically five (5) business days, and sometimes as long as seven to ten (10) business days. The bank\'s cited justifications typically include:
188: 
189: > • Internal processing requirements, including the need to update account authorization profiles in the bank\'s core banking system;
190: >
191: > • Coordination across multiple bank departments --- operations, compliance, legal, and relationship management --- each of which may need to review and approve the transition of account control;
192: >
193: > • The complexity of freezing automated payment instructions, including ACH origination agreements, wire transfer templates, standing payment orders, and sweep account configurations, which may require manual intervention; and
194: >
195: > • Regulatory and compliance review, including potential Bank Secrecy Act / Anti-Money Laundering considerations if the NOEC results in changes to the account\'s beneficial ownership or authorized signers.
196: 
197: In the current Ironbridge matter (Hargrave Stein internal reference 2025-HSC-04417), Ironbridge National Bank, N.A. has proposed a five (5) business-day compliance period in its Turn 1 markup of the ACA. Blackmere Fox LLP, bank counsel, has cited the bank\'s internal processing protocol and the involvement of multiple departments as the basis for the extended period.
198: 
199: **[4.3 --- Acceptable Fallback Positions (Yellow)]{.underline}**
200: 
201: **Authorized Fallback --- Three (3) Business Days Maximum.** Pinnacle\'s deal team has pre-authorized a maximum NOEC compliance period of three (3) business days. This represents the outer boundary of acceptability without further client approval and reflects the deal team\'s assessment that a three-business-day period provides adequate time for the bank\'s operational transition while limiting Pinnacle\'s exposure to dissipation risk during the compliance window.
202: 
203: The following sample counter-language should be used:
204: 
205: > *\"The Bank shall comply with the Secured Party\'s instructions with respect to the Accounts beginning no later than the third (3rd) Business Day following the Bank\'s receipt and authentication of a Notice of Exclusive Control delivered in accordance with Section \[●\].\"*
206: 
207: **Negotiation Tactic.** Open with the preferred two-business-day position in the first counter-markup. If the bank rejects the two-business-day period (which is likely, given that Ironbridge has proposed five business days), offer three business days in the second counter-markup as a \"significant concession\" to close the issue. Frame the concession as movement toward the bank\'s position (from two days to three days, representing a 50% increase in the compliance window) and emphasize that this represents Pinnacle\'s final position. Avoid moving directly from two days to five days, as doing so forfeits negotiating leverage on this issue and signals willingness to accept the bank\'s initial position.
208: 
209: **[4.4 --- Walk-Away / Escalation Triggers (Red)]{.underline}**
210: 
211: > • Any NOEC compliance period exceeding three (3) business days requires express approval from Diana Whitford before the negotiator may agree. The negotiator should present the escalation with the following information: (a) the bank\'s stated rationale for the longer period, (b) the total controlled deposit balances at stake, and (c) an assessment of the dissipation risk during the extended compliance window.
212: >
213: > • If the bank insists on five (5) or more business days, escalate and assess whether the delay risk is proportionate to the controlled deposit balances at stake. In a matter where total controlled deposits are in the range of \$38 million --- as in the current Graycliff Industries/Ironbridge National Bank transaction, where the three controlled accounts (●●●●-4471, ●●●●-4472, and ●●●●-4473) hold approximately \$38,150,000 in aggregate --- a five-business-day delay could expose Pinnacle to material dissipation risk, particularly if the borrower is aware that a NOEC has been delivered and is motivated to divert funds before the lock-down takes effect.
214: 
215: **[SECTION 5 --- CONFLICTING INSTRUCTIONS AND PRIORITY WATERFALL]{.underline}**
216: 
217: **[5.1 --- Pinnacle\'s Preferred Position (Green)]{.underline}**
218: 
219: Pinnacle\'s form ACA provides that in the event of conflicting instructions from the Secured Party and the Depositor regarding the disposition of funds in the controlled accounts, the Secured Party\'s instructions shall prevail in all circumstances, both before and after delivery of a NOEC.
220: 
221: This priority waterfall operates in two distinct contexts:
222: 
223: > **Pre-NOEC Context.** Prior to NOEC delivery, the Secured Party priority operates as a latent backstop. Because Pinnacle does not ordinarily issue instructions prior to a triggering event, conflicts between Pinnacle\'s instructions and the Depositor\'s instructions are unlikely in practice during the ordinary-course period. However, if they arise --- for example, because Pinnacle has delivered a standing instruction restricting certain types of transfers, or because Pinnacle has issued an instruction in connection with a cash management dispute that does not rise to the level of an Event of Default --- Pinnacle\'s instructions control, and the bank must follow them.
224: >
225: > **Post-NOEC Context.** After delivery of a NOEC, the Depositor\'s instruction rights are fully extinguished; the bank must comply exclusively with the Secured Party\'s instructions. In this context, the conflict scenario does not arise as a practical matter because the Depositor has no instruction rights to exercise. However, the form language is drafted broadly to ensure that any residual or unauthorized Depositor instruction is subordinated to the Secured Party\'s instruction.
226: 
227: The form language addressing conflicting instructions is as follows:
228: 
229: > *\"In the event of a conflict between instructions received from the Secured Party and instructions received from the Depositor, the Bank shall follow the instructions of the Secured Party.\"*
230: 
231: This language is intentionally broad and unconditional. It does not distinguish between the pre-NOEC and post-NOEC periods, does not require the Bank to inquire into the basis for the conflict, and does not give the Bank discretion to determine which instruction to follow. The simplicity of the provision is a feature, not a limitation --- it eliminates ambiguity and ensures that the Bank has a clear, unqualified contractual directive.
232: 
233: **[5.2 --- Common Bank Pushback]{.underline}**
234: 
235: Banks frequently resist unconditional Secured Party priority in the conflicting-instructions waterfall, particularly prior to NOEC delivery. The bank\'s concern is primarily operational and relates to its relationship with the Depositor as its customer. The bank\'s typical arguments include:
236: 
237: > • The Depositor is the bank\'s customer and the account holder; prior to NOEC delivery, the Depositor\'s instructions should control in the ordinary course because the Depositor is the party that established the banking relationship and that the bank owes its primary duties to.
238: >
239: > • The bank does not want to be caught between competing instructions from two parties, both of whom are the bank\'s contractual counterparties, without a clear contractual framework that protects the bank from liability for following one party\'s instructions over the other\'s.
240: >
241: > • Unconditional Secured Party priority prior to NOEC delivery could disrupt the Depositor\'s ordinary-course business operations and potentially trigger claims by the Depositor against the bank for failure to honor the Depositor\'s payment instructions.
242: 
243: A common bank markup is to provide that prior to NOEC delivery, the Depositor\'s instructions control (because the Depositor is the account holder and the bank\'s customer), and that Secured Party instructions take priority only after NOEC delivery. Some banks further condition post-NOEC priority on the bank\'s completion of its internal NOEC processing period (see Section 4 above), which effectively creates a gap period during which neither the Secured Party\'s nor the Depositor\'s instructions have clear contractual priority.
244: 
245: **[5.3 --- Acceptable Fallback Positions (Yellow)]{.underline}**
246: 
247: **Fallback A --- Bifurcated Priority (Pre- and Post-NOEC).** Accept a bifurcated structure that distinguishes between the pre-NOEC and post-NOEC periods. Under this structure: (i) prior to NOEC delivery, the Depositor\'s instructions control in the ordinary course, but the bank agrees to promptly notify Pinnacle of any instruction from the Depositor that conflicts with a standing instruction previously delivered by Pinnacle; and (ii) upon and after NOEC delivery, Pinnacle\'s instructions control exclusively and without qualification. The following sample language may be offered:
248: 
249: > *\"Prior to the Bank\'s receipt of a Notice of Exclusive Control, the Bank shall follow the instructions of the Depositor with respect to the Accounts; provided that if the Bank receives an instruction from the Depositor that conflicts with a standing instruction previously delivered to the Bank by the Secured Party, the Bank shall promptly notify the Secured Party of such conflict and shall follow the Secured Party\'s standing instruction. Upon and after the Bank\'s receipt of a Notice of Exclusive Control, the Bank shall follow exclusively the instructions of the Secured Party and shall not be required to follow any instructions of the Depositor.\"*
250: 
251: This bifurcated structure is a reasonable compromise that addresses the bank\'s concern about pre-NOEC operational disruption while preserving Pinnacle\'s exclusive post-NOEC control. The notification obligation in the pre-NOEC period provides Pinnacle with visibility into potential conflicts and allows Pinnacle to take action (including issuing a NOEC if warranted) before the conflict results in dissipation of collateral.
252: 
253: **Fallback B --- Minimum Protective Language.** If Fallback A is rejected by the bank --- which is unusual, as the bifurcated structure is generally accepted by bank counsel --- accept a pre-NOEC regime in which Depositor instructions control without a standing-instruction override, but require the bank to agree that it will not permit any withdrawal, transfer, or disposition of funds from any Account in an amount exceeding a specified threshold without providing Pinnacle at least two (2) business days\' prior written notice. The threshold should be specified on a per-transaction basis and should be calibrated to the total controlled deposit balances; as a general guideline, the threshold should be set at the greater of \$500,000 or 5% of the aggregate account balances as of the date of the ACA. This fallback does not give Pinnacle instruction priority in the pre-NOEC period, but it provides an early-warning mechanism that enables Pinnacle to monitor large withdrawals and to deliver a NOEC if the withdrawal activity suggests dissipation.
254: 
255: **[5.4 --- Walk-Away / Escalation Triggers (Red)]{.underline}**
256: 
257: > • Any bank markup that conditions post-NOEC compliance with Pinnacle\'s instructions on Depositor consent, Depositor notice, or any third-party approval --- **hard stop**. This undermines UCC § 9-104 control and is not negotiable. The post-NOEC period is the critical juncture at which Pinnacle\'s control must be absolute, and any qualification of that control defeats the purpose of the ACA.
258: >
259: > • Any bank markup that gives the bank discretion to determine which conflicting instruction to follow --- rather than a contractually mandated waterfall --- **hard stop**. A discretionary standard (e.g., \"the Bank may, in its sole discretion, determine which instruction to follow\") is unacceptable because it introduces uncertainty into the priority scheme and leaves Pinnacle\'s collateral protection subject to the bank\'s judgment call at the moment of conflict.
260: >
261: > • Any markup that requires Pinnacle to indemnify the bank for following Pinnacle\'s instructions in a conflicting-instructions scenario --- **escalate to Diana Whitford**. This is likely acceptable if limited to post-NOEC instructions and subject to the indemnification parameters described in Section 8 of this playbook (including the carve-out for the bank\'s gross negligence, willful misconduct, or bad faith). However, an open-ended indemnification that covers the bank\'s losses for following Pinnacle\'s instructions in all circumstances --- including situations where the bank\'s own negligence contributed to the loss --- is not acceptable.
262: 
263: **[SECTION 6 --- BANK SET-OFF RIGHTS]{.underline}**
264: 
265: **[6.1 --- Pinnacle\'s Preferred Position (Green)]{.underline}**
266: 
267: Pinnacle\'s form ACA requires full subordination of the bank\'s liens and set-off rights in the controlled accounts to the Secured Party\'s security interest. The form language provides:
268: 
269: > *\"The Bank hereby subordinates all liens, security interests, encumbrances, claims, counterclaims, and rights of set-off that the Bank may now or hereafter have in or with respect to the Accounts and the funds on deposit therein to the security interest of the Secured Party.\"*
270: 
271: The rationale for this provision is straightforward: Pinnacle\'s security interest in the controlled accounts should be first-priority. If the bank can exercise set-off rights against controlled account balances --- for example, to satisfy unpaid loan obligations, treasury management fees, or other amounts owed by the Depositor to the bank --- Pinnacle\'s collateral can be diminished without notice to or consent of Pinnacle, potentially at the very moment when the borrower is in financial distress and the collateral is most needed to support Pinnacle\'s recovery. Full subordination eliminates this risk by ensuring that the bank\'s claims are junior to Pinnacle\'s security interest in all circumstances.
272: 
273: The priority rule of UCC § 9-327 reinforces Pinnacle\'s position: under § 9-327(1), a security interest held by a secured party that has control of a deposit account has priority over a conflicting security interest held by a secured party that does not have control. However, under § 9-327(3), a security interest held by the depository bank itself has priority over a security interest held by another secured party, even if the other secured party has control. This means that absent a contractual subordination, the bank\'s own security interest in the deposit account --- which arises by operation of the bank\'s relationship with the depositor --- would have priority over Pinnacle\'s security interest. The subordination provision in the ACA is designed to contractually override this statutory priority rule by requiring the bank to subordinate its claims. UCC § 9-339 permits such subordination by agreement.
274: 
275: **[6.2 --- Common Bank Pushback]{.underline}**
276: 
277: Banks virtually always resist full subordination of their set-off rights. The negotiation of the set-off provision is typically one of the most contentious aspects of ACA negotiation and often consumes a disproportionate share of the negotiation timeline. Common bank positions include:
278: 
279: > • **Preservation of Set-Off for All Depositor Obligations.** The bank seeks to preserve its right of set-off for \"any obligation owed to the Bank by the Depositor, whether direct or contingent, now existing or hereafter arising.\" This formulation is maximally broad and would permit the bank to set off against controlled account balances for obligations arising under credit facilities, loan agreements, letter of credit reimbursement obligations, treasury management agreements, and any other banking relationship between the bank and the Depositor --- including contingent or unliquidated obligations.
